title: A family cuts its energy use: refrigerator and furnace

stimulus.title: A household's energy upgrades

table.caption: Energy data for one household (invented data for practice; the carbon dioxide factors are near published values)
rows: Carbon dioxide from the local grid
Natural gas burned by the old furnace
Energy in 1 therm of natural gas
Carbon dioxide from burning natural gas

stimulus.text: A family in a cold-winter state is deciding how to cut its energy use. Show every setup with numbers and units. Efficiency = useful energy out ÷ energy in × 100.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the percent decrease in yearly electricity use when the family replaces the old refrigerator with the new one. Show your setup.

rubric.point: A correct setup with the difference in brackets divided by the old value: (1,100 - 400) / 1,100 × 100.
accept: (400 - 1,100) / 1,100 × 100 with the answer stated as a decrease

rubric.point: Correct answer with units: about 63.6% (accept 63% to 64%).

parts.sample: Percent decrease = (old - new) / old × 100 = (1,100 kWh - 400 kWh) / 1,100 kWh × 100 = 63.6%. Electricity use for the refrigerator decreases by about 63.6%. (Writing (new - old) / old × 100 = -63.6% earns the same points.)

mistakes.why: Divide by the old value (1,100 kWh), the starting point, not the new one.
Multiply by 100 to turn the fraction into a percent.
Also right on the exam: a -63.6% change is a 63.6% decrease. This checker asks for the size of the decrease, (1,100 - 400) / 1,100 × 100.
You divided by the new value (400). Percent change divides by the old value, 1,100.
Also right on the exam: a -63.6% change is a 63.6% decrease. This checker asks for the size of the decrease, 63.6%.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide, in kg, the new refrigerator avoids each year. Show your setup with units that cancel.

rubric.point: A correct setup with units: (1,100 kWh - 400 kWh) × 0.4 kg / 1 kWh.
Correct answer with units: 280 kg of carbon dioxide per year.

parts.sample: Electricity saved = 1,100 kWh - 400 kWh = 700 kWh per year. Carbon dioxide avoided = 700 kWh × (0.4 kg / 1 kWh) = 280 kg of carbon dioxide per year.

mistakes.why: That is the old refrigerator's total. Use the electricity saved: 1,100 - 400 = 700 kWh.
You divided. Multiply kWh by kg per kWh so kWh cancels.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: The old furnace burns 900 therms a year at 80% efficiency. Calculate how many therms the new 95% efficient furnace would burn to deliver the same heat to the house. Show your setup.

rubric.point: A correct setup: heat delivered = 900 therms × 0.80, then therms needed = (900 × 0.80) / 0.95.
Correct answer with units: about 758 therms per year (accept 757 to 758.5).

parts.sample: Heat delivered by the old furnace = 900 therms × 0.80 = 720 therms of useful heat. The new furnace needs 720 therms ÷ 0.95 = about 758 therms of natural gas per year to deliver the same heat.

mistakes.why: That is what the new furnace would deliver from 900 therms. First find the heat the house needs (900 × 0.80), then divide by 0.95.
The efficiencies are swapped. Heat needed = 900 × 0.80; gas for the new furnace = that ÷ 0.95.
That is 900 × 0.95, the heat the new furnace makes from the old amount of gas. Divide the needed heat by 0.95 instead.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the money the family saves each year on natural gas with the new furnace. Use your answer from part (c). Show your setup.

rubric.point: Correct setup and answer with units: (900 - 758) therms × \$1.40/therm ≈ \$199 per year (accept \$198 to \$200, or a value consistent with part (c)).

parts.sample: Therms saved = 900 - 758 = 142 therms. Money saved = 142 therms × (\$1.40 / 1 therm) ≈ \$199 per year.

mistakes.why: That is the cost of running the new furnace. Savings use the therms saved: 900 minus the new furnace's therms.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why burning natural gas in the new furnace still contributes to climate change, even though it is more efficient.

rubric.point: Explains that burning natural gas (methane) still releases carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat, so emissions fall but are not zero.
accept: combustion of methane produces carbon dioxide
natural gas is a fossil fuel; efficiency lowers but does not end carbon dioxide release

parts.sample: Natural gas is mostly methane, a fossil fuel, and burning it combines its carbon with oxygen to make carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the atmosphere. The new furnace burns less gas for the same heat, so emissions fall by about 750 kg a year, but every therm it burns still releases about 5.3 kg of carbon dioxide.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Propose one change, other than replacing the furnace or the refrigerator, that would further reduce the family's home heating energy, and justify how it works.

rubric.point: Proposes a specific, realistic change other than a new furnace or refrigerator: adding attic insulation, sealing drafts and weather stripping, installing efficient windows, a programmable thermostat set lower at night, or a ground source heat pump.
accept: lowering the thermostat setting in winter
planting a windbreak on the north side

rubric.point: Justifies how it works: less heat escapes (or less heating is needed when no one is home), so less gas is burned for the same comfort.
accept: insulation slows heat flow through the attic so the furnace runs less
a heat pump moves heat from the ground instead of burning gas

parts.sample: The family should add insulation to the attic and seal drafts around windows and doors. Insulation slows the flow of heat out of the house, so the furnace runs fewer hours to keep the same temperature and burns less natural gas.
